 Jackery made its portable power stations even smaller
 The new Jackery Explorer 100D puts a longer lasting lithium iron phosphate battery in the palm of your hand.﻿
 The new Jackery Explorer 100D puts a longer lasting lithium iron phosphate battery in the palm of your hand.﻿
 by Andrew Liszewski 
 Andrew Liszewski
 Senior Reporter, News
 Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.
 Follow See All by Andrew Liszewski 
 Nov 2, 2026, 5:00 AM UTC 
 Image: Jackery 
 Andrew Liszewski 
 Andrew Liszewski
 Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.
 Follow See All by Andrew Liszewski 
 is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid. 
 Jackery announced a new portable power station that uses the safer and longer-lasting lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries the company first introduced in 2023. But what makes the new Explorer 100D stand out is that it’s Jackery’s smallest power station to date, measuring only 4.6 by 3.4 by 3.4 inches and weighing just 1.87 pounds. Its size and 96Wh (30,000mAh) of battery capacity means you can squeeze it into your carry-on and power multiple devices during a long flight.
 The Jackery Explorer 100D will be available starting November 15th through Walmart for $99. The power station is already available from Costco if you don’t want to wait, but only in a two-pack for $179.99. You can definitely find smaller and cheaper 30,000mAh portable chargers, but the LFP cells in the 100D are “engineered for up to 8 years of regular use,” according to Jackery, with a 3,000 charge cycle lifespan, so it should easily outlast competing products that use more common lithium-ion battery cells.
 Image: Jackery 
 Although the 100D is considerably smaller and lighter than Jackery’s other portable power stations , the company still includes an integrated handle and offers an optional shoulder strap for carrying it around. On the front, you’ll find a pair of 140W USB-C ports, plus an additional 18W USB-A port, but the 100D maxes out at 158W of total output, so power delivery across the ports will be reduced when all three are in use. If you need to charge it, can’t find an outlet, and managed to find room to also pack a solar panel, the 100D supports up to 100W of direct solar input, which will charge it back up to 80 percent capacity in about an hour and a half.

 EcoFlow has been a consistent top-performer in our tests, with one model earning the top spot in our guide to portable power stations. High-capacity, durable build, and reliable output are all strong with this line.
 So, the EcoFlow Delta 3 Classic with 45W solar panel for $479 (was $598) at Best Buy is an easy recommendation. If a power outage leaves you without heat controls, internet, or a working fridge, the Delta 3 Classic gives you a quiet, fume-free backup you can keep indoors.
 • Best for: Professionals, campers, and RV owners who want dependable backup power for outages or portable power on the go.
 • Why we like it: Beyond the strong performance in our tests, this EcoFlow model features 1,024Wh of long-life LFP battery capacity, 1,800W of continuous AC output to run big appliances, 3,000 charge cycles, and a five-year warranty. The solar panels for off-grid use sweeten this one considerably for us.
 • What you need to know: At $479 it’s good value for the battery alone, though the small panel is more of a bonus for added energy security rather than a serious charging option.
 Save $119
 Ecoflow Delta 3 Classic: was $598 now $479 at Best Buy A 1,024Wh portable power station with a lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery rated for 3,000 cycles, 1,800W of continuous AC output with a 3,600W peak, and a weight of 26.7 pounds. This bundle includes a 45W solar panel and a protective bag, and it comes with a five-year warranty. EcoFlow sells and ships it through Best Buy’s marketplace.
 View Deal 
 Why We Recommend It
 EcoFlow is one of the biggest names in portable power, and the Delta 3 Classic is a pared-back version of its Delta 3 that keeps the essentials: a large, long-lasting LFP battery and enough output to run a full-size fridge or a space heater for a while. We haven’t tested this model ourselves, so this pick rests on EcoFlow’s track record and our experience testing other models. Expect fast charging, easy of use, and total dependability if you need additional or on-the-move power supply. The five-year warranty adds welcome peace of mind for a product you may rely on in an emergency.
 For more top picks, see our guide to the best portable power stations . 
 Price Context & Historical Value
 This is $119, or 20%, off the bundle’s $598 list price, which is a solid discount on a 1kWh power station with a five-year warranty. Keep in mind that the included 45W panel would take more than a full day of ideal sunlight to refill the battery, so think of it as a top-up tool rather than a full-blown charging solution. If you want backup power in place before winter, this is a good time to buy.
 Should you buy it?
 ✅ Buy the EcoFlow Delta 3 Classic bundle if... you want reliable backup power for outages, you need enough output to run a fridge, router, or CPAP machine, or you value a long-life LFP battery with a five-year warranty.
 ❌ Skip the EcoFlow Delta 3 Classic bundle if... you plan to rely on solar charging, since a 45W panel is far too small to refill this battery quickly, you need a power station that’s easy to carry long distances at 26.7 pounds, or you’d prefer to buy directly from Best Buy rather than a marketplace seller.

 If you're looking for a portable power station that can keep essential equipment running through an outage or provide electricity on a road trip, I've found a huge $470 discount on the Bluetti Elite 100 V2 with a 100W solar panel for $629 (was $1099) at Amazon .
 The Elite 100 V2 packs a 1024Wh LiFePO4 battery into a relatively compact 25-pound unit and delivers 1800W of continuous AC output. It can power up to 11 devices simultaneously, and Bluetti rates the battery for more than 4,000 cycles. It can reach 80% charge in around 45 minutes and fully recharge from AC power in about 70 minutes.
 This bundle also includes a 100W solar panel, giving you a way to boost the battery when you're camping or away from the grid. A full solar charge lasts around seven hours, under suitable conditions obviously..
 Save $470
 Bluetti Solar Generator Elite 100 V2 With 100w Solar Panel, 1024wh 1800w: was $1,099 now $629 at Amazon This 1024Wh LiFePO4 power station delivers 1800W AC output, powers up to 11 devices, supports fast AC charging and 10ms UPS backup, and includes a 100W solar panel.
 View Deal 
 Why we recommend it
 In his four-star review of the Elite 100 V2, our expert Jack called it a "small, light-weight, portable yet powerful power station" and liked that it is quiet when fans are running, has a very good app and high wattage output.
 The Elite 100 V2 strikes a useful balance between capacity, output, and portability. At 25 pounds and around 12.6 x 8.5 x 9.8 inches, it's reasonably manageable for a 1kWh-class power station, with a hidden handle making it easier to carry.
 The UPS function can switch over in 10ms or less during a power failure, helping keep equipment such as a PC or Wi-Fi router running. Bluetti also rates operating noise as low as 30dB, which should make it less intrusive indoors.
 An AC connection can take the battery to 80% in around 45 minutes and fully recharge it in roughly 70 minutes, so you don't have to leave it plugged in for most of the day before it's ready to go.
 For more options, take a look at our roundup of the best portable power stations .
 Price context & historical value
 The Bluetti Elite 100 V2 and 100W solar panel bundle is currently reduced from $1,099 to $629, a $470 cut of around 43%.
 This isn't the lowest price we've seen it however. The bundle was reduced to $550 in November 2025, for Black Friday , making the current deal $79 more expensive than that previous low.
 It's still a large reduction from the listed price though, and we'd definitely recommend considering buying it now.
 Should you buy it?
 ✅ Buy the Bluetti Elite 100 V2 if... 
 You want a portable power station that can cover camping trips, road trips, and emergency backup duties at home. This model's 1024Wh capacity is more than enough for charging your various devices. The 1800W continuous output also allows it to run a wide range of household equipment.
 The included solar panel will make the bundle especially appealing for camping and off-grid use. You can boost the battery without access to mains power, and the panel is included rather than being an additional purchase.
 ❌ Skip the Bluetti Elite 100 V2 if... 
 You only need something to keep phones, tablets, and other small electronics charged. A 1024Wh power station has more capacity than those jobs require, and a smaller model will be cheaper and considerably lighter.
 The included 100W solar panel also isn't particularly powerful compared with the capacity of the battery. Bluetti quotes around seven hours for a full solar recharge under suitable conditions, so anyone relying heavily on solar power may want a higher-output compatible panel.
 The Catch: What to know before you buy 
 The 100W solar panel ships separately from the power station, so don't be concerned if the entire bundle doesn't arrive in a single delivery.
 It's also worth distinguishing between the various power figures in the listing. The Elite 100 V2 provides 1800W of normal AC output, while Bluetti also lists higher figures for Power Lifting and surge capability. Those shouldn't be treated as the amount of continuous power available for everyday use.

results.text:
Bluetti Sora 500 review: I tested this 500W solar panel 
 Skip to main content 
 We handpick every product we feature. We may be compensated or earn commission from the links on this page.
 Shopping 
 I tested Bluetti’s Sora 500, and it recharged my 2,000Wh power station in a day
 This 500-watt foldable panel delivered 463 watts in my test and recharged a 2,000Wh power station in a day, though setup takes patience.
 By Tony Carrick , Special to Hearst Oct 26, 2026 
 Bluetti’s Sora 500 unfolds into 12 panels arranged in two rows.
 Tony Carrick Portable solar panels are an essential sidekick to my portable power station on camping trips, helping me keep the lights on, the RV fridge running, and the water pump operating longer. But while they can add days to a dry camping trip, their small size and average efficiency often lack the muscle to charge larger  portable power stations . You can solve this with larger solar panels or by daisy-chaining a few sets together, but then portability becomes an issue. Multiple sets of solar  panels get bulky, and I don’t want a campsite that looks like a solar farm. 
 Bluetti’s Sora aims to change that with its new Sora 500 solar panels , which put out up to 500 watts in a surprisingly compact size. I spent several weeks testing these solar panels to see how quickly they could charge my Bluetti 2,000-watt-hour power station. With their compact size and efficient design, they quickly earned a permanent spot on my off-grid camping equipment list. 
 Bluetti BLUETTI Sora 500W Solar Panel 
 $799.00 at bluettipower.com 
 Portability
 If you’re taking solar panels on the road for off-grid camping, you'll want them as compact and easy to carry as possible, and the Sora 500s are. The Sora panels weigh 28.4 pounds and fold down into a 22.4-inch by 17.5-inch square that’s just 3.3 inches thick. This makes them heavier than comparable portable solar panels, including the Jackery SolarSaga 500X and Zoupe bifacial panels, but their square shape keeps them more compact and easier to carry than bulkier panels that weigh a few pounds less. They slide easily among other camping gear in a trunk or storage.   
 At 28.4 pounds, the Sora 500 packs small but still takes effort to carry.
 Tony Carrick Impressive efficiency equals ample power output
 Power output matters for whether a set of solar panels can really extend a power station's life, whether you’re off-grid RVing or trying to keep the fridge and lights on during a lengthy power outage. Portable solar panels can be tricky because they often get significantly less than their rated max wattage than bifacial glass solar panels. Many factors sap a solar panel’s efficiency, including wiring, high temperatures, angle, and cloudy skies. As a result, you typically get only 75% to 85% of a solar panel’s rated output. 
 During testing, I found Bluetti’s Sora solar panels performed well above average. On a clear, sunny day with temperatures in the mid-seventies, they generated 463 watts (93% efficiency) at midday. By repositioning the panels periodically for optimal sun exposure, I fully recharged my 2,000Wh portable power station on a day with scattered cloud cover. It’s impressive performance for such compact Sora panels. 
 The panel folds accordion-style and snaps together for storage.
 Tony Carrick Setup can be frustrating 
 Anyone who's used portable solar panels knows they can be frustrating to set up, especially if you don't have another set of hands to help. The  Sora panels are no exception. The panels consist of two rows of six solar panels stacked on top of each other. They use four supports that pull out from the back of the solar panels, plus additional supports that sit on top of the top-row supports. The design works, but folding out all four legs to support the panels was frustrating. I set up the panels in a few minutes, but a second set of hands would have made it much easier. 
 In my experience, soft portable solar panels tend to sag in places, which can hurt performance and give the panels a sloppy, low-tech look. That's not the case with the Sora 500 panels. Once I set them up, they sat straight with no noticeable sagging. 
 Connecting to the Bluetti AC200 I used to test the solar panels was easy, in part because both were from the same brand.I also connected them to an Anker Solix C2000 Gen 2 portable power station I was testing, though I needed an adapter cable. 
 While setting up the Sora panels was a little tedious, taking them down was easy. The legs fold flat and snap securely to the panels. Once flat, the panels fold easily in an accordion style. I didn’t have to fold and refold to get it right. Once assembled, snap straps hold the panels together. I had the whole set folded up and on the move in under a minute on the first try. 
 Who is it for?
 Bluetti’s solar panels have many applications. They break down to a small size yet still produce a lot of power, making them a great option not only for keeping an RV powered while dry camping but also for emergency backup power if you live off the grid or in a place where outages are frequent and long. Pulling the panels out of the garage, setting them up, and connecting them to a power station takes minutes. Once up and running, they pull enough power to keep a 2,000 to 3,000Wh power station going for days, depending on the weather. Like most soft portable solar panels, the Sora 500s are made from rugged material. You can wedge them into other gear in the back of a truck or in a garage without worrying about damaging them. 
 It’s a heavy panel with a fussy setup, but for RVers and off-grid campers who need to recharge a large power station, the Sora 500’s compact fold and strong output make the tradeoff worthwhile.

results.title: How to build a seriously comfortable car camping setup
results.snippet: The article explains how to create a comfortable car-camping setup by prioritizing shelter, good sleep, easy meals, lighting, cooling, seating, and cleanup without overpacking. Because gear travels by car, campers can choose roomy tents, thick sleeping pads, full-size bedding, sturdy cookware, and larger comfort items, while still considering campsite dimensions and vehicle cargo space. It compares recommended products across categories, including family tents and compatible footprints; insulated or compact sleeping pads, sleeping bags, pillows, and blankets; two-burner stoves, cookware, grill
results.text:
How to build a comfortable car camping setup: Essential gear 
 Skip to main content 
 We handpick every product we feature. We may be compensated or earn commission from the links on this page.
 Shopping 
 How to build a seriously comfortable car camping setup
 From roomy tents to better bedding and an organized camp kitchen, here’s the gear that makes a weekend outdoors feel like a getaway.
 By Shannon Ullman , Special to Hearst Oct 28, 2026 
 The right tent, sleeping gear, camp kitchen and other comforts can turn a basic car camping trip into a more relaxing weekend outdoors.
 Billy Cadden Some camping is about bringing what you need to get through the night; other camping lets you actually settle in. With your car parked nearby, you don’t have to carry everything on your back or cram it into a tiny pack. You can bring a mattress thick enough to sleep on your side, a cooler with ingredients for a real breakfast, and a chair you’ll happily sit in for hours.
 That doesn’t mean bringing half your house into the woods. A comfortable car camping setup is about choosing the few things that make the biggest difference once you’re there: staying dry, sleeping well, eating easily, and having a place to relax at the end of the day.
 The trick is knowing what deserves that extra space in your car. Below, I’ll break down a comfortable setup, from shelter and sleep to cooking, lighting, cooling, seating, and cleanup, with product recommendations for each.
 Everything you need for the comfiest car camping setup 
 Shelter and weather protection
 Car camping doesn’t have to mean sleeping in your car. A tent gives you room to stretch out, change clothes, and keep your vehicle free for gear storage or a day trip. Since you won’t be carrying it far, you can choose a roomier tent with enough height to stand up in and space for thicker bedding. Look beyond the number of people on the label: think about where bags will go, how much room you’ll need to pitch it, and whether the rainfly will keep the entrance dry when the weather turns. Here are a few products we’d recommend:
 Six-person or family camping tents
 A roomy tent can make car camping feel much more comfortable, especially when you want space for thick sleeping pads , bags, and a place to change clothes standing up. These three serve different groups: the Snow Peak is best for a couple or small family, the Teton gives larger groups the most space for the money, and the KingCamp is built for a longer, more elaborate stay.
 Best overall: Snow Peak Alpha Breeze 
 Best budget tent: Teton Hacienda 8-Person Family Tent 
 Upgrade: KingCamp Khan Villa 4-Season Bell Tent 
 Best overall: Snow Peak Alpha Breeze 
 Snow Peak Alpha Breeze 
 $549.95 at snowpeak.com 
 The Snow Peak Alpha Breeze is a roomy three-season tent for two campers or a small family, with a three- to four-person capacity, doors on all four sides, a 6-foot-1-inch peak height, and a vestibule that converts into an awning. Its airflow, headroom, and sheltered entrance make it comfortable for car camping, though the 22-pound tent takes more effort to pitch than a basic dome and costs more than the larger Teton.
 Best budget tent: Teton Hacienda 8-Person Family Tent 
 TETON Hacienda 8-Person Family Tent 
 $399.99 at tetongear.com 
 The Teton Hacienda is a spacious, three-season tent with an eight-person capacity, nearly vertical walls, and an 82-inch peak height that leaves room for cots and gear. A swinging door, full-coverage rainfly, and interior storage add convenience at a budget-friendly price. At about 38 pounds with a roughly 10-foot-8-inch square footprint, it needs a large campsite close to the car, and smaller groups will have more room for bedding and luggage.
 Upgrade: KingCamp Khan Villa 4-Season Bell Tent 
 KingCamp KingCampKHAN VILLA4-Season 4-6Person BellTent 
 $999.99 at kingcampoutdoors.com 
 The KingCamp Khan Villa is a four-season tent for four to six campers, with two sleeping areas, a central living space, and a 94-inch peak height. Its pole-free middle makes furnishing and moving around easier, while polycotton fabric, mesh windows, and adaptable walls help manage ventilation. At nearly 59 pounds and with a roughly 15-by-10-foot footprint, it’s best for longer stays when you need plenty of vehicle and campsite space. Using its stove opening requires following the manufacturer’s installation and safety instructions.
 Tent footprints and weather protection 
 A footprint goes beneath your tent to help protect its floor from rocks, grit and repeated use. It’s a small addition that can be especially worthwhile when you’ve invested in a tent you plan to use for years. Fit matters more than the label on the package: the footprint should sit beneath the tent floor, not stick out where it could collect rain. These picks fit different tents; they are not interchangeable with the three family tents above.
 Best overall for a compatible MSR tent: MSR Universal Footprint 
 Affordable for Kelty Wireless 4 owners: Kelty Wireless 4 Footprint 
 Upgrade for Copper Spur UL3 owners: Big Agnes Copper Spur UL3 Footprint 
 Best overall for a compatible MSR tent: MSR Universal Footprint 
 MSR MSR Universal Tent Footprint, 2 Person 
 $54.95 at amazon.com 
 The MSR Universal Footprint adds a lightweight, packable layer beneath compatible MSR tents to protect the floor from abrasion and keep it cleaner during pack-up. It comes in multiple sizes, so check MSR’s size chart for your exact tent model and confirm the selected variant in the listing before ordering. Despite its name, it doesn't fit every tent and shouldn't be assumed to fit the Snow Peak, Teton, or KingCamp models above.
 Affordable for Kelty Wireless 4 owners: Kelty Wireless 4 Footprint 
 Kelty Wireless 4 Footprint
 $39.95 at rei.com 
 The Kelty Wireless 4 Footprint protects the matching tent’s floor without the measuring or folding a generic tarp requires. Made from 68-denier polyester, it measures 92 by 82 inches, weighs 14 ounces, and includes color-coded corner connections and a carry bag. It’s an affordable, straightforward addition for Wireless 4 owners, though it needs separate drying and storage when damp and won’t fit the larger family tents above.
 Upgrade for Copper Spur UL3 owners: Big Agnes Copper Spur UL3 Footprint 
 Big Agnes Copper Spur UL3 Footprint
 $100.00 at rei.com 
 The Big Agnes Copper Spur UL3 Footprint protects the matching tent’s floor and enables its Fast Fly setup, using just the footprint, poles, stakes, and rainfly. Made from coated ripstop nylon, it weighs seven ounces and measures 90 inches long, tapering from 70 to 62 inches wide. It’s a lightweight option for campers who also backpack, though it costs considerably more than the Kelty footprint and requires the compatible Copper Spur UL3.
 Sleeping pads for a more comfortable car camping setup 
 A good sleeping pad does two jobs: cushions you from uneven ground and slows heat loss. Since you’re carrying it in a car, you can choose a thick foam-filled pad even if it takes up more space. Consider an air pad when the trunk is crowded, or you want to use the same gear on trips away from the car. Only the Teton below is self-inflating; the other options require inflation.
 Best overall for car camping: Teton Sequoia Self-Inflating Sleeping Pad 
 Best for saving vehicle space: Sea to Summit Ether Light XR Insulated 
 Best overall for car camping: Teton Sequoia Self-Inflating Sleeping Pad 
 TETON Sequoia Self-Inflating Sleeping Pad 
 $83.99 at tetongear.com 
 The Teton Sequoia pairs three inches of foam with a self-inflating valve and stretch-fabric surface for a cushioned sleeping setup. It comes in a 78-by-26.8-inch single size weighing 5.51 pounds, or a 52-inch-wide Mammoth version for two sleepers weighing 10.45 pounds. Both have a listed R-value of 7 for cold-ground insulation. Inflation takes little effort, but these pads are bulky, especially the Mammoth, so leave plenty of space in your car and tent.
 Best for saving vehicle space: Sea to Summit Ether Light XR Insulated 
 Sea to Summit Ether Light XR Insulated Air Sleeping Pad 
 $189.00 at seatosummit.com 
 The Sea to Summit Ether Light XR is an insulated air pad with nearly four inches of cushioning, an R-value of 4.1, and a stuff sack that doubles as a pump. The regular size measures 72 by 22 inches, weighs 18.5 ounces, and packs to about 8 by 4 by 4 inches, making it useful when cargo space is tight. Rectangular wide options offer more sleeping room, though they cost and weigh more. It requires inflation and care around sharp ground.
 Sleeping bags, blankets and camp pillows 
 A thick pad is only part of a comfortable bed. Your sleeping bag needs to suit the overnight temperature, and your pillow needs to support the way you actually sleep. Car camping also leaves room for an extra blanket you can use by the fire before bringing it into the tent. These picks serve different purposes, so think of them as parts of a sleep setup rather than alternatives.
 Best sleeping bag for restless sleepers: Marmot Wraptor Down 30 
 Best roomy sleeping bag: White Duck Slumbernest 
 Best packable pillow: Klymit Luxe Pillow 
 Best foam pillow: Wise Owl Outfitters Camping Pillow 
 Best small extra blanket: Rumpl Fleece Puffy Mini Blanket 
 Best full-size camp blanket: Nomadix Graphene Puffer Blanket 
 Best sleeping bag for restless sleepers: Marmot Wraptor Down 30 
 Marmot Wraptor Down 30° Sleeping Bag
 $279.00 at marmot.com 
 The Marmot Wraptor Down 30 uses overlapping flaps secured at the shoulder and hip instead of a long side zipper, giving restless sleepers more freedom to move. A foot vent helps release heat, while 650-fill-power down keeps it relatively compact at about 2 pounds, 4 ounces. The closure may take getting used to, and its tested comfort rating is 35°F despite the “30” name, so consider the forecast and your sleeping pad’s insulation for chilly nights.
 Best roomy sleeping bag: White Duck Slumbernest 
 White Duck Outdoors Slumbernest™ Sleeping bag
 $110.00 at whiteduckoutdoors.com 
 The White Duck Slumbernest offers a roomy, bedlike setup with a soft flannel lining, synthetic insulation, and a two-way zipper that opens fully for use as a blanket. It measures 78 by 34 inches and comes in 0°F, 20°F, 30°F, and 50°F versions, weighing roughly 4.7 to 8 pounds. Its generous footbox and pillow space suit car camping, though it’s bulky and heavy. Choose the temperature version that matches your trip.
 Best packable pillow: Klymit Luxe Pillow 
 Klymit Klymit Luxe Pillow 
 $36.97 at amazon.com 
 The Klymit Luxe pairs an inflatable core with a soft cover, offering adjustable firmness in a compact camp pillow. It weighs approximately seven ounces, though specifications vary by version. It’s useful when car space is tight and softer than a bare air pillow, but requires inflation and may not feel as comfortable as your pillow from home.
 Best foam pillow: Wise Owl Outfitters Camping Pillow 
 Wise Owl Outfitters Wise Owl Outfitters Camping Pillow 
 $32.31 at amazon.com 
 The Wise Owl Snoozy pillow pairs memory foam with a soft microsuede cover for a familiar feel without inflation. It compresses into a drawstring bag and comes in small (12 by 16 inches, nine ounces) and medium (14 by 18 inches, 11 ounces) sizes. It takes up more space than an inflatable pillow, but suits campers who prefer foam, with the medium offering extra room for restless sleepers.
 Best small extra blanket: Rumpl Fleece Puffy Mini Blanket 
 rumpl.com Fleece Puffy Blanket Seascape Cream 
 $139.95 at rumpl.com 
 The Rumpl Fleece Puffy Mini combines a soft fleece lining with a water-resistant topside for a cozy extra layer for kids, pets, or your lap around camp. It’s machine washable and includes a stuff sack and a clip for wearing over your shoulders. Its compact size makes it easy to keep in the car, but it offers limited coverage for adults and won’t replace proper sleeping bedding.
 Best full-size camp blanket: Nomadix Graphene Puffer Blanket 
 Nomadix Graphene Puffer Blanket: Grand Canyon 
 $99.95 at nomadix.co 
 The Nomadix Graphene Puffer Blanket measures 55 by 74 inches, with snap-together sides you can wear around camp or use to form a loose sleeping-bag shape. Its moisture-resistant ripstop shell and anchorable corners suit picnics, lounging on a chair, and extra warmth in the tent. Machine washable and weighing two pounds, it packs to 15 by 7 by 6 inches. It’s versatile but has no standardized sleeping-bag temperature rating, so use it as an extra layer on cold nights.
 Two-burner camping stoves 
 A two-burner camping stove lets you make coffee while breakfast cooks, or keep a pot warm while you finish dinner in a skillet. For car camping, the choice comes down to how much cooking space you want, how the stove packs, and whether you’d rather bring your own pots or buy a complete system. All three are for outdoor use; check each model's fuel requirements before your trip.
 Best overall: Camp Chef Everest 2X 
 Best compact option: Optimus Gemini II 
 Upgrade: Jetboil Genesis Basecamp System 
 Best overall: Camp Chef Everest 2X 
 Camp Chef Everest 2X 
 $229.99 at campchef.com 
 The Camp Chef Everest 2X is a suitcase-style propane stove with two independently controlled 20,000-BTU burners, push-button ignition, and 215 square inches of cooking space. Its broad surface lets you cook with two pans at once, making it practical for couples or groups who want to use their own cookware. It takes up more table and cargo space than a folding stove, and you buy cookware separately.
 Best compact option: Optimus Gemini II 
 Optimus Optimus Gemini II Two-Burner Propane Camping Stove 
 $199.95 at amazon.com 
 The Optimus Gemini II packs two independently controlled burners into a slim, folding stove with wind protection and a pressure regulator. It weighs about 26.8 ounces and folds to roughly 12 by 2.76 by 4.14 inches, making it useful when trunk space is tight, though large pans may crowd each other. It uses compatible EN417 fuel cartridges rather than standard one-pound propane bottles. Confirm you’re buying the Gemini II, since the earlier Gemini model was recalled.
 Upgrade: Jetboil Genesis Basecamp System 
 Jetboil Jetboil Genesis Basecamp System, Gray | Holiday Gift 
 $399.95 at rei.com 
 The Jetboil Genesis Basecamp System pairs a folding two-burner propane stove with a 5-liter pot, 10-inch ceramic-coated frying pan, and carry bag that keeps everything packed together. Its two 10,000-BTU burners offer simmer control and push-button ignition, making it a convenient kitchen setup for campers starting from scratch. It costs considerably more than a stove alone, so its value depends on whether you need the included cookware. Fuel is sold separately.
 Compact camping cookware 
 A two-burner stove makes cooking possible; the right kitchen kit makes it less chaotic. For car camping, you can bring sturdy cookware without worrying about every ounce, but nesting or roll-up pieces still leave more room for food and the rest of your gear. The two cooksets below are alternatives for two people. The utensil roll and wash basin each fill a different role alongside either one.
 Best organized utensil kit: Dometic Front Runner Camp Kitchen Utensil Set 
 Best overall cookset for car camping: Sea to Summit Detour Five-Piece Cookset 
 Best space-saving cookset: Sea to Summit Frontier Ultralight Five-Piece Cookset 
 Best cleanup addition: Sea to Summit Ultra-Sil Kitchen Sink 
 Best organized utensil kit: Dometic Front Runner Camp Kitchen Utensil Set 
 Dometic Front Runner Series Camp Kitchen Utensil Set 
 $55.96 at dometic.com 
 The Dometic Camp Kitchen Utensil Set packs 24 pieces into a canvas roll that hangs near your cooking area for easy access. It includes a bamboo cutting board, knives, cooking and serving tools, a bottle opener, and place settings for four. It’s a convenient way to keep a family or group’s utensils organized, though it may duplicate supplies you already own and adds more pieces to wash. Pots and pans are not included.
 Best overall cookset for car camping: Sea to Summit Detour Five-Piece Cookset 
 Detour Detour Stainless Steel One Pot Cook Set - (5 Piece) 
 $200.95 at seatosummit.com 
 The Sea to Summit Detour five-piece cookset nests a 3-liter stainless-steel pot, two bowls, and two mugs into a compact package for two campers. The pot’s three-ply base promotes even heating and works on gas or induction stoves, and it holds pasta, soup, or one-pot meals. The set weighs about 2 pounds, 13.5 ounces, and packs to roughly 9 by 8 by 3 inches. It’s heavier and pricier than the Frontier, and includes no frying pan or cooking utensils.
 Best space-saving cookset: Sea to Summit Frontier Ultralight Five-Piece Cookset 
 Sea to Summit Frontier Ultralight One Pot Cook Set 2L - [5 Piece] 
 $114.95 at seatosummit.com 
 The Sea to Summit Frontier five-piece cookset nests a 2-liter aluminum pot, two bowls, and two cups, with a removable handle that locks everything together for travel. The pot has a ceramic nonstick coating, a strainer lid, and a clip to hold the lid aside while cooking. At 18.6 ounces and roughly 7 by 6 by 4 inches packed, it suits simple meals for two and trips where space matters, though the smaller pot and coated surface require some care.
 Best cleanup addition: Sea to Summit Ultra-Sil Kitchen Sink 
 Sea to Summit Ultra-Sil Kitchen Sink 
 $44.95 at seatosummit.com 
 The Sea to Summit Ultra-Sil Kitchen Sink is a collapsible 10-liter basin with carrying handles that makes washing dishes and transporting wastewater easier. It weighs about 2.5 ounces and packs into a roughly 5-by-5-by-1-inch pouch. The lightweight basin needs to be mostly full to stand unsupported and handles water up to 140°F, so avoid boiling water and dispose of wastewater according to campground rules.
 Portable grills 
 A portable grill can make dinner feel less like a camp chore, especially if you’d happily use it for tailgating or backyard meals, too. The question is whether it earns its space alongside your stove and cooler. These three take different approaches: the Weber has a stand and can feed a group, and the Snow Peak lets you cook over a fire before gathering around it afterward.
 Best overall for families: Weber Traveler Portable Gas Grill 
 Upgrade for campfire cooking: Snow Peak Takibi Fire & Grill 
 Best overall for families: Weber Traveler Portable Gas Grill 
 Weber WEBER TRAVELER® Portable Gas Grill 
 $449.00 at weber.com 
 The Weber Traveler offers 320 square inches of cast-iron grilling space, a 13,000-BTU burner, and a wheeled stand that folds with one hand. Its freestanding design keeps the picnic table clear, making it practical for family or group cookouts. At 49 pounds, it’s heavy and bulky, so measure your cargo space before buying. It has one burner and uses disposable propane cylinders (sold separately).
 Upgrade for campfire cooking: Snow Peak Takibi Fire & Grill 
 Snow Peak Takibi Fire & Grill
 $349.95 at rei.com 
 The Snow Peak Takibi combines a stainless-steel fire pit with a grill bridge and grate for cooking dinner and gathering around afterward. It weighs 32 pounds, measures roughly 18 by 18 by 12 inches when assembled, and packs into an included carry bag. It’s best for campers who enjoy tending a fire, though it requires fuel and cleanup, plus a separate coal-bed accessory for charcoal cooking. Check current campground fire rules and whether portable fire pits are permitted before bringing it.
 Hard-sided and wheeled coolers 
 A cooler is one of the first things to claim space in a car, so choose its size after you’ve planned your meals. A couple bringing breakfast ingredients and a few drinks has different needs from a family packing two days of food. Also consider how far you’ll carry it from the parking spot: a large cooler is much less convenient once it’s full.
 Best for family trips: Ninja FrostVault 65-Quart Wheeled Cooler 
 Upgrade for a compact setup: Oyster Tempo Cooler 
 Best for family trips: Ninja FrostVault 65-Quart Wheeled Cooler 
 Ninja Ninja FrostVault 65qt Wheeled Cooler with Dry Zone 
 $349.99 at amazon.com 
 The Ninja FrostVault 65-Quart Wheeled Cooler pairs an ice-filled main compartment with a separate chilled drawer that keeps food away from meltwater and easy to reach. Its capacity suits families or groups, while wheels and a reinforced handle make transport easier. At 38.8 pounds empty and roughly 36.5 by 17.8 by 18.9 inches, it needs substantial cargo space. Follow Ninja’s packing instructions and monitor perishable food temperatures, since the drawer’s cooling depends on how you pack and use the cooler.
 Upgrade for a compact setup: Oyster Tempo Cooler 
 Oyster Oyster Performance Cooler 
 $395.00 at oystercooler.com 
 The Oyster Tempo uses thin-walled, insulated aluminum to fit about 24 quarts of capacity into a compact cooler weighing 12.3 pounds. It includes a carrying strap and suits couples trying to save cargo space, though its high price and modest capacity limit its appeal for larger groups. It doesn't actively refrigerate food, so pack contents cold, use ice packs for perishables, and monitor temperatures. Oyster’s ice packs and aluminum carry handle are sold separately.
 Rechargeable and solar lanterns 
 Good campsite lighting does more than help you find your shoes. Put a lantern near the cooking area so you can see what you’re doing, then bring a softer light into the tent when it’s time to wind down. Rechargeable models save you from disposable batteries, while solar charging is a useful backup if you get enough daylight.
 Best overall: Goal Zero Lighthouse 600 
 Best for campsite atmosphere: BioLite AlpenGlow 500 
 Best compact solar option: LuminAID Max Quick Inflate 
 Best overall: Goal Zero Lighthouse 600 
 Goal Zero Goal Zero Lighthouse 600 Lantern & USB Power Hub 
 $69.95 at rei.com 
 The Goal Zero Lighthouse 600 provides up to 600 lumens of adjustable light, illuminating the whole lantern or just one side. A handle and collapsible legs make it useful on a picnic table or around camp. It weighs about 1 pound, 2 ounces and recharges by USB or hand crank, with solar charging available through a separate panel. Its USB output can charge a small device in a pinch, though that reduces the battery available for lighting.
 Best for campsite atmosphere: BioLite AlpenGlow 500 
 BioLite BioLite Alpenglow Multicolor USB Lantern with Rechargeable Battery and Charging Port, Alpenglow 500 
 $79.95 at rei.com 
 The BioLite AlpenGlow 500 delivers up to 500 lumens in white, warm, and colorful modes, making it useful for both cooking and relaxed evenings at camp. It sits on a table or hangs from its loop, casting light in all directions. Its rechargeable battery lasts up to five hours on high, so charge it before your trip and use lower settings when you don’t need full brightness.
 Best compact solar option: LuminAID Max Quick Inflate 
 Luminaid LuminAID Max Quick Inflate Solar Lantern with Phone Charger 
 $49.95 at rei.com 
 The LuminAID Max Quick Inflate lantern packs flat and twists open to provide up to 200 lumens of soft light, making it useful for a tent, table or backup illumination. It includes a built-in solar panel and USB phone-charging output. Recharge it via USB in about two hours or with 16 hours of sunlight, so charge it at home and top it off with solar. It saves space but lacks the brightness needed for a large group campsite.
 Portable power stations 
 Start by deciding what needs power. Charging phones and headlamps for two nights is a very different job from running a fan or a larger appliance. Battery capacity, measured in watt-hours, helps you compare them; the output rating tells you whether a station can run a particular device. Charge your portable power station before leaving, even if it accepts solar panels.
 Best for a typical weekend: Jackery Explorer 300 
 Best small backup: Patriot Power Voyager XL 
 Upgrade for larger power needs: BLUETTI AC200P L 
 Best for a typical weekend: Jackery Explorer 300 
 Jackery Jackery Explorer 300 
 $289.00 at amazon.com 
 The Jackery Explorer 300 provides 293 watt-hours of capacity and 300 watts of output, with AC and USB connections for phones, lights, cameras or a small fan. It’s a practical weekend option when a pocket power bank won’t cover everyone’s charging needs, though it takes up more cargo space. Check your devices’ wattage before packing, since it's best suited to small electronics rather than prolonged use of power-hungry appliances.
 Best small backup: Patriot Power Voyager XL 
 4Patriots Patriot Power Voyager XL Solar Power Bank 
 $299.00 at walmart.com 
 The Patriot Power Voyager XL packs 96 watt-hours of capacity and 120 watts of continuous output into a roughly 2.1-pound unit, with an AC outlet and other charging connections. It’s useful for phones, headlamps, and small electronics, though its capacity is about a third of the Jackery’s, limiting runtime for devices such as fans. It recharges from a wall outlet or compatible solar panel; check your package to see whether a panel is included.
 Upgrade for larger power needs: BLUETTI AC200P L 
 BLUETTI BLUETTI AC200P L Portable Power Station | 2,400W 2,304Wh 
 $1399.00 at bluettipower.com 
 The Bluetti AC200P L offers 2,304 watt-hours of capacity and 2,400 watts of rated output for campers running multiple devices or equipment with higher power needs. It can also work at home, but its price and size make it hard to justify for a two-night trip focused on phone charging. Check your equipment’s wattage and expected runtime before investing; additional power equipment is sold separately.
 Camp chairs and loveseats 
 A chair’s packed size is easy to overlook until you’re trying to fit four of them next to a cooler. Consider how long you’ll sit in it, whether you want to sit close to the fire, and how easily you can get up. The four linked products are individual chairs; none is a loveseat.
 Best sturdy chair: YETI Trailhead 
 Best low chair: Kelty Lowdown 
 Best compact high-back chair: Helinox Sunset Chair 
 Best reclining chair: NEMO Stargaze Evo-X 
 Best sturdy chair: YETI Trailhead 
 YETI Camp Chair 
 $300.00 at yeti.com 
 The Yeti Trailhead Camp Chair combines a supportive mesh-style seat with a folding frame, grippy feet, and an adjustable cup holder for long evenings around camp. It has a 16.75-inch seat height and includes a carry bag, but folds down to roughly 43 x 10 x 8 inches. That long packed shape takes up more cargo space than a compact chair, so check your trunk dimensions before buying several.
 Best low chair: Kelty Lowdown 
 Kelty Kelty Lowdown Chair 
 Buy at amazon.com 
 The Kelty Lowdown is a low-profile folding chair suited to lounging around a fire pit with your feet stretched out. Its relaxed seating position works well for evenings at camp, though it sits too low for comfortable dining at a standard picnic table. Campers who find low seats difficult to get out of should choose a taller chair.
 Best compact high-back chair: Helinox Sunset Chair 
 Helinox Helinox Sunset Chair (re) 
 $189.95 at amazon.com 
 The Helinox Sunset Chair combines a high back, higher seat, and ventilated fabric with a collapsible frame that saves trunk space. It weighs about 3 pounds, 10.5 ounces, packs to 18.5 by 6 by 4.5 inches, and has a listed 320-pound capacity. It offers back support and is easier to rise from than a low chair, though it requires assembly and lacks the cushioning of a padded lounge chair.
 Best reclining chair: NEMO Stargaze Evo-X 
 NEMO Equipment NEMO Equipment Stargaze EVO-X Folding Reclining Camp Chair 
 $134.95 at amazon.com 
 The NEMO Stargaze Evo-X folds open on a six-point-contact frame and reclines as you shift your weight, with a padded headrest for leaning back. Its quick setup and reclining design suit long evenings of chatting or stargazing. It’s bulkier than a compact pole-frame chair, though, and its moving feel may not appeal to everyone.
 Outdoor blankets 
 A blanket can make a campsite feel much more inviting, but these three do different jobs. The Rumpl and YETI are made to spread on the ground, while the insulated Kelty is best for pulling over two people on a chilly night.
 Best packable ground mat: Rumpl Everywhere Mat 
 Upgrade ground blanket: YETI Lowlands 
 Best warm blanket: Kelty Biggie 
 Best packable ground mat: Rumpl Everywhere Mat 
 Rumpl Rumpl Everywhere Mat 
 $79.95 at amazon.com 
 The Rumpl Everywhere Mat pairs a soft microsuede top with a waterproof bottom for picnics, dewy grass or keeping shoes and bags off the ground beside your tent. Corner pockets hold small items, and an attached carrying case keeps packing simple. Sizes vary by version, and spot-cleaning is recommended. It’s a versatile ground cover but offers little insulation for warmth at night.
 Upgrade ground blanket: YETI Lowlands 
 YETI Lowlands Blanket 
 $200.00 at yeti.com 
 The Yeti Lowlands Blanket combines a plush surface with a waterproof underside for comfortable lounging on damp ground. Designed to repel dirt and pet hair, it’s useful for campsites and dog-friendly picnics. It’s machine washable and dryable and includes a carry bag, but it takes up more cargo space than a thin mat and is better suited for ground use than for cold-night warmth.
 Best warm blanket: Kelty Biggie 
 Kelty Kelty | Biggie Blanket 
 $54.95 at amazon.com 
 The Kelty Biggie is an oversized, synthetically insulated blanket with a soft brushed side, a more weather-resistant reverse and an included stuff sack. Sized to cover a double- or queen-size airbed, it works well as a shared extra layer for couples or families, whether draped over chairs or bedding. It takes up more space than a thin mat and doesn’t replace an insulated sleeping pad.
 Portable fans and cooling products 
 A fan won’t turn a hot tent into an air-conditioned room, but moving air can make sleeping and sitting through a still summer evening more pleasant. Check its power source, runtime, and how you’ll position it. A fan clipped beside one person serves a different purpose than one that circulates air for the group.
 Best campsite fan: NESTOUT FAN-1 Full Kit 
 Affordable fan and light: Odoland Camping Lantern With Ceiling Fan 
 Best campsite fan: NESTOUT FAN-1 Full Kit 
 NESTOUT FAN-1 Portable Fan (Full Kit) 
 $89.99 at nestout.com 
 The Nestout FAN-1 kit includes a fan, tripod, clamp, and carry case, and you can stand, hang, or mount it around camp. Four speeds, three oscillation angles, adjustable tilt, and a shutoff timer let you direct airflow toward a chair or sleeping area. Its flexible setup adds more to pack, and the battery sells separately, so bring a compatible power bank or another supported power source.
 Affordable fan and light: Odoland Camping Lantern With Ceiling Fan 
 Odoland Odoland Portable LED Camping Lantern with Ceiling Fan 
 $18.99 at amazon.com 
 The Odoland combines a small fan and LED lantern in a compact unit that hangs inside a tent, saving space and providing both airflow and overhead light. It’s suited to a personal sleeping area rather than cooling an entire campsite. Check the selected listing’s battery requirements and runtime before your trip.
 Water bottles and hydration gear 
 An easy-to-reach bottle makes it more likely everyone will drink water throughout the day. Pack enough potable water for drinking, cooking, and cleanup, then decide whether you need insulation, a bottle that shrinks as you use it, or a purifier for water collected away from camp.
 Best everyday camp bottle: Dometic Chug Bottle 
 Best packable day-trip bottle: HydraPak Flux 32 oz. 
 Best for treating collected water: Grayl GeoPress 24 oz. 
 Best everyday camp bottle: Dometic Chug Bottle 
 Dometic Dometic 34 oz Insulated Chug Bottle 
 $44.99 at amazon.com 
 The Dometic Chug Bottle holds 1 liter (about 34 ounces) and uses vacuum-insulated stainless steel to keep drinking water cold. Its leakproof lid, rubber base, and dishwasher-safe design make it useful for hikes, camp, and everyday use. It stays bulky when empty and won’t replace a larger container for cooking and dishwashing.
 Best packable day-trip bottle: HydraPak Flux 32 oz. 
 HydraPak HydraPak Flux - Collapsible Backpacking Water Bottle (1 Liter) 
 $29.00 at amazon.com 
 The HydraPak Flux is a lightweight, 32-ounce flexible bottle that stands when full and compresses as it empties, making it easy to pack for day hikes and fold away afterward. It saves space in your bag or car, though it lacks insulation and feels less rigid than a conventional bottle.
 Best for treating collected water: Grayl GeoPress 24 oz. 
 GRAYL GRAYL GeoPress 24 oz Water Purifier Bottle 
 $99.95 at amazon.com 
 The Grayl GeoPress is a 24-ounce bottle with a press-action purifier and replaceable cartridge for treating collected water on remote outings or trips without reliable drinking water. Follow Grayl’s treatment instructions and cartridge replacement schedule. It costs more than a standard bottle and requires ongoing cartridge purchases, so it’s most useful when your plans call for water purification.
 Storage totes and gear organizers 
 A good storage system speeds up camp setup because you know where the stove fuel, lantern, and clean forks are. Car camping gives you room for a sturdy box or tote, but measure your cargo area before committing to several. Pack by activity so you can pull out a single container when you need it.
 Best small gear box:   Gregory Alpaca Gear Box 25 
 Best flexible container: RUX 40L 
 Best open-access tote: Kitworks Gear Tote 
 Best small gear box:   Gregory Alpaca Gear Box 25 
 Gregory Gregory Alpaca 25L Camp Gear Storage Box 
 $59.95 at amazon.com 
 The Gregory Alpaca Gear Box is a rigid, 25-liter container with a clear lid, making it easy to find lights, utensils, first-aid supplies, and other small camp essentials . It weighs about 4.7 pounds and measures roughly 19.9 by 17.3 by 7.9 inches, making it easy to stack and keep packed between trips. Its fixed shape takes up the same cargo space even when partly empty and is less practical for bulky bedding.
 Best flexible container: RUX 40L 
 RUX RUX 40L 
 $250.00 at Amazon 
 The RUX 40L is a flexible, weather-protective gear container for bedding, clothing, or shared camp supplies. Its adaptable shape and generous capacity suit families or campers whose gear changes from trip to trip. It comes at a premium price and offers less built-in organization than a compartmentalized box, so give it a clear packing purpose to avoid overloading it.
 Best open-access tote: Kitworks Gear Tote 
 My Kit Works Gear Tote 
 $159.00 at mykitworks.com 
 The Kitworks Gear Tote stands open with a wide mouth for easy access to kitchen supplies or shared family gear. It comes in 35- and 55-liter sizes weighing 2.5 and 3.5 pounds, respectively, with optional organizers sold separately. It’s convenient for items you use throughout the day, though accessories add cost, and a fully loaded tote can be heavy.
 First-aid kits and basic safety equipment 
 Keep safety gear in a known spot, not buried under the tent at the bottom of the trunk. A first-aid kit handles routine injuries; a weather radio and vehicle tools address different problems. Check the supplies and charge any batteries before leaving, especially when your campsite is beyond cell service.
 Best portable first-aid kit: Adventure Medical Kits Ultralight/Watertight   
 Best vehicle first-aid kit: Surviveware First Aid Kit 
 Best weather information tool: Midland ER310PRO Radio 
 Best vehicle tool: NOCO Boost Air 
 Best portable first-aid kit: Adventure Medical Kits Ultralight/Watertight 
 Adventure Medical Kits Adventure Medical Kits Ultralight/Watertight Medical Kit .7 
 $44.95 at amazon.com 
 The Adventure Medical Kits Ultralight/Watertight packs bandages, blister care, and other first-aid basics in water-protected packaging that weighs about 5.8 ounces. Sized for up to three people over three days, it’s easy to keep accessible at camp or carry on a day hike. Supplies are limited, so review the contents and add personal medications or anything else your group needs.
 Best vehicle first-aid kit: Surviveware First Aid Kit 
 Surviveware Surviveware Waterproof Premium First Aid Kit 
 $79.99 at amazon.com 
 The Surviveware First Aid Kit offers an organized, more substantial set of supplies for camping and road trips. Store it where everyone can reach it without unpacking, and check the selected version’s contents before buying, since kits vary. Add any medications or supplies your family needs, and account for overlap if you also carry a hiking kit.
 Best weather information tool: Midland ER310PRO Radio 
 Midland Midland - ER310PRO, Portable Emergency Bluetooth Weather AM/FM Radio 
 Buy at amazon.com 
 The Midland ER310PRO receives NOAA weather alerts without cell service and includes a 10,000 mAh rechargeable battery, USB-C device charging, and Bluetooth audio. It’s useful for remote trips, though weather-radio reception varies by location. Charge it and learn the controls before leaving, and treat its device-charging function as a backup rather than your main power source.
 Best vehicle tool: NOCO Boost Air 
 NOCO NOCO Boost Air AX65: 2000A Jump Starter with 22A 100 PSI Air Compressor 
 $209.94 at Amazon 
 The NOCO Boost Air combines a portable jump starter and tire inflator, so it can handle a dead battery or low tire, making it useful for drives to remote campsites. Specifications vary across the series, so choose a model rated for your vehicle, learn its controls, and keep it charged. It adds cost and cargo bulk but can earn its place on trips far from roadside help.
 Two-night car camping packing checklist 
 Shelter 
 Tent and rainfly
 Tent poles, stakes and guylines
 Footprint that fits the tent
 Sleep 
 Sleeping pad or mattress for each person
 Sleeping bag or bedding for each person
 Pillow for each person
 Extra blanket if nights will be cool
 Food and cooking 
 Meals and snacks for two nights and three days
 Cooler, ice or ice packs
 Camp stove or grill
 Correct fuel and a lighter
 Pot, pan, and cooking utensils
 Plates or bowls, cups, and eating utensils
 Cutting board and knife
 Water and cleanup 
 Drinking water or a plan to use potable water at the campground
 Water bottles for everyone
 Water for cooking and washing up
 Dish soap, sponge, and wash basin
 Trash bags
 Paper towels or dish towels
 Campsite comfort 
 Chair for each person
 Lanterns or other camp lights
 Charged power bank or power station, if needed
 Fan or outdoor blanket, if useful for the forecast
 Clothing and personal items 
 Clothes for the forecast, including a warm layer and rain protection
 Sleepwear and extra socks
 Toiletries and toilet paper
 Sunscreen and insect repellent
 Medications
 Before you leave 
 Check the weather forecast and overnight low
 Confirm the campground’s water, fire, and food-storage rules
 Charge lights, fans and power banks
 Check stove fuel and cooler ice
 Pack a first-aid kit and vehicle essentials
 Confirm the tent and cooler fit in the car with the rest of your gear

77 Best Items For Your Emergency Kit 2026 | The Strategist 
 Every product is independently selected by (obsessive) editors. Things you buy through our links may earn us a commission. 
 77 items in this article 
 11 items on sale! 
 Photo-Illustration: The Strategist; Photos: Retailers 
 Compiling a stash of emergency-preparedness items used to be a task many of us kept on the back burner — something we knew was important and we’d get to eventually. But eventually, we now know, might be closer than anyone thought. And while we’re not suggesting you start digging out an underground bunker and filling it with instant noodles , in the past few years we’ve come to learn that having a few things on hand before you need them will only help you, even if it’s just mentally.
 Most preppers, like Oregon’s Afrovivalist , Sharon Ross, equate preparation with peace of mind. “Once a person is prepared during a disaster,” she says, “they don’t feel the sense of urgency to go shopping for supplies.” So if visions of empty store shelves still haunt you, have a nice, calm look at our well-organized, detailed list of emergency supplies to keep on hand. To assemble it, we consulted recommendations from the CDC ,  Red Cross , the Department of Homeland Security , and the NYC Emergency Management Department . But those agencies give you only general categories, and we wanted specifics. So we interviewed 22 survivalists, preppers , bushcrafters , homesteaders , and emergency professionals about their favorite things to always have on-hand — and their advice to make your bugout (or bugin) the best it can possibly be.
 Here are their suggestions, broken down into categories based on your level of survivalist instinct. There’s a lot to sift through here, but you can pick and mix products according to your needs. For many, a leaner survival kit makes more sense than a military-grade one. “Simplicity is key when prepping,” says Prepper Press founder Derrick James. Especially as, in a worst-case scenario, you might have to haul all of this gear a considerable distance. “It’s really important for people to know what their limitations are,” says emergency preparedness expert Aton Edwards, author of the book Preparedness Now! “Don’t prove how strong you are by dragging around a 40-pound bag . Rage lift in the gym, don’t rage lift your bag.” And in any potential urban or wilderness survival situation, advises Steve Lancia of North Camp Survival School in the Hudson Valley, there’s one piece of gear you should always keep around: “A cool head.”
 Updated on October 28, 2026 
 We’ve updated this list to make sure our top emergency picks are still available and correctly priced. 
 If you’re not quite ready to build your own bunker, check out our first-time homeowners’ guide to getting prepared , and if you’re just getting started, we’ve got a list of 10 essentials you should stock for any emergency . 
 The Basics 
 Backpack
 Most preppers keep two bags : a three-day bag and a two-week bag. While you needn’t get too hung up on that, it’s not a terrible idea to have something that you can easily grab that has everything you need in it in case you have to leave quickly. Bushcrafter Mark Christensen recommends a “quality rucksack, or even a five-gallon bucket , which keeps your emergency gear together.” Survivalist E.J. “Skullcrusher” Snyder (whom you might know from his many appearances on Naked and Afraid ) likes the “tough and roomy” bags by Gregory , but if you prefer something more tactical, he suggests something by Maxpedition . Jim Cobb , editor-in-chief of Prepper Survival Guide and Backwoods Survival Guide magazines, likes the RUSH24 bag from 5.11 Tactical, saying that it’s “robust without being ridiculously huge.” And Lisa Bedford, a.k.a. the Survival Mom , loves the Presidio Tactical Assault Backpack from Flying Circle, because it’s “a very good size for teens and most women.”
 Edwards suggests an alternative to traditional rucksacks: the humble folding shopping cart . “If you aren’t physically fit, then lugging around a fully stocked go-bag can be difficult,” he explains. “So a folding cart will let you move around from one shelter to another shelter.”

 Survivalist Travis McGill, along with Thomas Coyne, the owner and lead instructor at Thomas Coyne Survival Schools , and a survivalist who asked that we refer to him by the pseudonym “RC” like Surefire flashlights because they’re virtually indestructible. They’re so durable, in fact, that some are specially designed to be used as a self-defense weapon, Coyne says. McGill uses the Surefire D3ft but admits “it’s totally overkill” and says you could also “get something that takes AA or AAA batteries since they’re easy to find and replace.” Even a small one for your keychain will do, says Mykel Hawke , a former U.S. Army special forces captain and author of several survival books . “But make sure it has a turn on button, not just squeeze on, for when you need to have light to work and be hands free,” he says. Cobb, Edwards, Snyder and Morgan Rogue of the prepper site Rogue Preparedness , however, prefer headlamps to flashlights so you can be 100 percent hands-free and there’s less chance you’ll put your torch down and lose it. Rogue likes Foxelli or Petzl , while Snyder uses a Black Diamond Spot 325 . Cobb also pointed us toward Streamlight’s products, which “work very well and will take a beating.”

And John Ramey of the prepper site theprepared.com likes the Leatherman Wave+ because it “doesn’t waste space and weight on tools that don’t matter much in an emergency, but it’s versatile and robust enough to be a core survival item.” The Signal , which McGill uses, also includes a fire starter and a whistle.  First-Aid Kit
 For most preppers, recommending a first-aid kit off the shelf would be like Julia Child telling you her favorite flavor of Pop-Tart. They like to put them together themselves so they can pack them with, as Hawke puts it, “some dressings for real trauma,” including tourniquets, Israeli Bandages , and, in R.C.’s case, zip-tie restraints, though he wouldn’t really say what those were for. That said, Coyne calls Adventure Medical Kits “the best first-aid kits on the market [and] definitely the closest commercially available to what I would customize for myself.” Survival Mom has a different preference, saying, “it would be hard to find better medical kits than those sold by Dr. Joe and Amy Alton at Doom & Bloom.” Their company offers a variety of kits that cover everything from labor to gunshot wounds. Whatever first aid kid you decide on, Mike Glover, crisis management and response expert and host of the popular FieldCraft Survival podcast , recommends you always maintain a 30-day supply of over-the-counter medicine (like painkillers , cold, allergy, anti-diarrheal medications) as well as any prescription medications. And another consideration, via Edwards: “There should be stuff for dental emergencies as well. Any kind of emergency that forces you to evacuate, especially in the city, you’re not going to be able to find a dentist.”

 Food
 Now hear us out: It might sound extreme, but at some point, you’ll probably wish you had some food. Our experts all approach the food question a little differently. Homesteader Lisa Sutton and the popular YouTuber, Prepper Potpourri (both Michiganers, both grandmothers), are big fans of canning and dehydrating . These processes take a little know-how, but are ultimately very practical and sustainable , especially if you grow your own food. They both like the All American Canner and the Excalibur Dehydrator . If you’re not ready to make your own food, our experts recommend stocking your pantry with, ideally, two-weeks’ worth of non-perishable foods like canned and dried goods, and peanut butter . “Think of very very simple meals, like oatmeal, [and] meals where you can open up a can of soup or chili and pour it over the rice and have more calories and more servings,” says Survival Mom, who goes into more detail about this in her book. And make sure you get stuff you actually like: “Don’t stock up on beans and rice if you don’t eat beans and rice,” Sutton says. Cobb’s in agreement: “Store what you eat and eat what you store. Don’t go out and buy cases of special ‘survival food’ if that’s not what you’re eating normally — a disaster or emergency is the last place you want to add stomach upset to the mix.”   
 If you want more variety and are thinking of supplementing your stock with freeze-dried food, Survival Mom, Prepper Potpourri, and David at Preppers Survive like Mountainhouse . Sutton recommends products from Thrive Life , “because they are real food, not prepackaged, high carb, high sodium emergency foods” like typical emergency foods tend to be. Hawke likes MRE’s (which aren’t technically freeze dried and which civilians can now buy), beef jerky , and meals from a company called Wise Foods, whose empty containers, he suggests, can be used as toilets. And don’t forget condiments, he says. R.C. recommends any junk food since it’s “full of sugar and preservatives and is good for survival,” if nothing else. Rogue suggests “morale-boosting foods” like macaroni and cheese, packaged cookies, raisins, dehydrated fruits, popcorn, and chocolate. And Edwards points us toward “high-protein stuff that’s not very heavy” like energy bars and trail mix. “Because when you’re in a crisis situation, you are going to burn more energy than you normally expend.”

 Water
 Jessica Kellog of the City of Los Angeles Emergency Management Department recommends having one gallon of water per person per day for seven days, but R.C. suggests getting even more: “You can’t have too much water,” he says. “If disaster strikes, the first thing I would do is fill the bathtub or the sink with water to keep it as a reserve.” As Edwards points out, “any kind of emergency where you have to evacuate your home, especially in a city, would probably classify as something that would disrupt water treatment.” If you’re sticking to bottled, any kind will do. But once that’s gone, you need to have a way to resupply, says Hawke. There are many ways to purify water . The easiest ways are by boiling (you’ll need something metal in which to do that), with water purification tablets (Coyne likes these ), and through various filtration systems . David likes LifeStraw’s one-gallon gravity bag that removes lead, parasites, bacteria, and chemicals. It can also be used as a straw alone, with a plastic bottle, or with in-line hydration bladders. If you need a smaller option, Survival Mom uses and recommends the Sawyer Mini. Edwards agrees that the Sawyer is “a really good filter, that’s one of the easiest and smallest to use.”

 A portable generator is one of those things you don’t much appreciate until you need it, whether that’s during a blackout following a storm or when your devices die on a camping trip. Fortunately, with many great portable generators on the market today, all you need is a bit of planning (and a few dollars) to never be without power again, whether you’re at home in the dark or out in the field.
 The picks below are based on expert recommendations and our own testing (done at campsites, at our homes, and even during a multiday blackout). Generators can be powered a few different ways: with gasoline, by burning both gas and propane, or even with the sun when you use solar power for a battery inverter generator — a newer option that’s a great choice if you’re looking to run a generator indoors.
 “Gas-powered generators create exhaust fumes, limiting the use to the outdoors,” says Corey Dandy, a manager with the hardware chain Aubuchon Company . “Battery generators are completely safe indoors or even in-tent.”
 What we’re looking for 
 Total capacity 
 The first thing to consider when shopping for a generator is just how much power it can store — and put out when you need it. A generator’s capacity is given in watt hours, a measure of energy that determines how much power a device can deliver, for how long. Essentially, it’s the amount of work a generator can do — for example, a generator rated at 100 watt hours could power a 100-watt lightbulb for one hour. (That would be a very small, weak generator!) Watt hours are given as a measurement of total capacity — a 4,000-watt-hour generator can deliver that amount of work starting from a full tank of gas or a full charge in its batteries.
 To figure out how big a generator you actually need, add up the watt hours required to run all your essential devices in an outage (or for an outing). Most manufacturers don’t list a device’s watt-hour consumption, so you’ll have to do some math: Multiply each product’s wattage (you can often find this on the appliance itself or online) by the number of hours you expect it to run. Some critical appliances, like a refrigerator, would need to run 24 hours, but you might only run a CPAP machine for eight hours. Not great at math? Kevin Feak, an engineer with Fire Protection and Safety Services , likes the simple generator calculators on sites like Lowe’s .
 But before you buy a generator that produces at least that number, you have to factor in surge. This is the temporary spike in electricity that appliances — especially those with compressors like refrigerators and window air conditioners — draw when they first start up before settling into a lower running wattage. “Surge numbers are really important to factor in when you’re sizing a generator,” says Feak. If two appliances with high surge-wattage demands attempt to turn on at the same time, it could overpower a weaker generator. Feak went on to say to ensure you factor in the surge demands for critical devices like medical equipment, sump pumps, and well pumps.
 Number and type of outlets 
 Many of the battery-power stations out there these days have myriad different outlets, from AC outlets, which are the same as those in the wall of your home, to USB and USB-C ports, for devices ranging from computers to phones, to direct current (DC) ports, which are often used to recharge a battery generator via a vehicle or solar panel. (You may recognize DC ports if you’ve driven a car with a cigarette lighter.) If you need a portable generator to keep multiple large home appliances running during a blackout, or even to charge an electric vehicle in a pinch, you’ll want a generator with several 120/240-volt AC outlets; if you just want to keep phones and lanterns charged, a much smaller unit with a few USB ports and an AC outlet or two is fine.
 If you regularly experience seasonal power outages but don’t have the budget for a larger whole-home standby generator, some of the bigger units we looked at (Feak advises looking for models with 240-volt output) can dish out enough power to run a whole house — but this requires the installation of a device called a transfer switch near your home’s main electrical panel. You’ll need to hire an electrician to install the switch itself (professional installation typically starts at around $500). Once installed, the transfer switch allows you to redirect power from the grid to the generator for the specific circuits you’ve selected by manually switching it over at the panel. Installing a transfer switch can be a worthwhile investment.
 Weight 
 Just because a generator isn’t permanently fixed in place doesn’t mean it’s necessarily portable . For this review, we’ve considered units that can reasonably be moved from place to place thanks to their lightweight or built-in wheels and handles, because the mobility of the hardware is of paramount importance here.
 Keep in mind that batteries are heavy, and for a comparable amount of power output, gas-powered generators — even when filled with fuel — are often lighter than battery-powered portable power stations. This is worth keeping in mind if you plan to charge with solar panels: Most panels include cables that are only about ten feet long, so unless you buy an extension cable, you may need to move the unit closer to wherever the panels can get maximum sunlight exposure. With some power stations weighing well over 100 pounds, that can mean hauling them up or down stairs and wheeling or carrying them across the yard.
 Best portable solar-powered generator overall

 EcoFlow Portable Power Station DELTA 3 Plus - With 220W Solar Panel
 $1,189 now 23% off 
 $919
 Capacity : 1024 watt hours / Outlets : 6 AC, 2 USB-A, 2 USB-C, 3 DC / Weight : 27.6 pounds (power station only; 64 pounds with 4 panels)
 EcoFlow’s Delta series has been a popular option since its launch in the roughly 1,000-watt-hour category, a segment that has since expanded to include models that now quadruple that capacity. The Delta 3 Plus is a Goldilocks pick, with the best combination of capability and ease of use we found in our testing. It’s capable enough out of the box to run critical appliances, light enough for one person to carry, has a very fast recharge time, has a user-friendly app, and can charge from multiple solar panels for extended use during outages.
 The Delta 3 Plus has a surge capacity of 3,600 watts, meaning it has an easier time starting demanding appliances, and it can recharge fully from a standard wall outlet in under an hour. In practical terms, that means in an emergency, charging the Delta 3 Plus for an hour at a friend’s house or a café can provide enough power to keep a standard refrigerator humming for about ten hours. If you want even more capacity, like many midsize power stations we tested, the EcoFlow can use additional batteries (they don’t have their own screens or ports) that stack on top, extending your storage and run time without the cost of another full Delta 3 Plus.
 The Delta 3 Plus’s real advantage is solar capability. While many units in this size class can handle around 500 watts of solar input, the Delta 3 Plus can accept up to 1,000 watts through two 500-watt inputs, meaning you can utilize more panels. That kind of solar capacity means that for a little more money, you can get closer to the kind of extended run time you’d expect from a gas or propane generator, but without the fumes, engine noise, or maintenance. EcoFlow offers both permanent rooftop panels and portable folding panels designed to store in a garage or basement and deploy in a yard during an outage. The portable versions avoid the need for professional installation (and let you take the whole system with you on the road).
 The Delta 3 Plus uses a standard XT60i connector, so you are not locked into EcoFlow-branded solar panels (though manufacturers often discount when you buy panels at the same time as the power station). A single 220-watt panel can recharge the 3 Plus in about seven or eight hours, though the unit does support pass-through charging, so it can still power appliances while it is recharging. Fully outfitted with four of EcoFlow’s 220-watt panels wired together in series, the unit can recharge in three to four hours under partly cloudy conditions, or in as little as two hours under sunny skies. EcoFlow’s bifacial panels collect energy from both sides and they perform best over reflective surfaces like snow, sand, or light-colored concrete rather than grass (slipping a mirror over the surface, under the panels, can boost efficiency).
 Each 220-watt panel weighs about 16 pounds and folds into a compact two-by-two-foot package roughly two inches thick, though unfurled it stretches into a strip that is seven feet long. Setup is straightforward, with built-in stands that help angle the panels between 30 and 60 degrees and simple plug-and-play connectors that make daisy-chaining panels together painless. Using four panels at once might make it look like a small solar farm spread across the yard, but even unfolded, the panels are manageable enough to store out of they way against a garage wall when they aren’t in active use.
 There are a few negatives: The included solar cable is only about eight feet long, however, which may make it difficult to keep the power station indoors while the panels sit outside in full sun. EcoFlow sells additional extension cables , but that’s another added expense. The real downside is cost: Building out a fast-charging solar setup adds up quickly, with each portable panel costing roughly $300, meaning a fully loaded array can add well over $1,000 to the overall system price, so choose a kit for the best deal.
 Looking for an even better deal? EcoFlow tells us that our former top pick, the Delta 2 , should be available through this summer. It’s still a very capable unit and can save you a little money if you don’t need the extra outlets and flexibility of the Delta 3 Plus.

 Weighing just under ten pounds with a flip-up handle, the Elite 30 V2 is a toaster-size power station built not just for emergency backup but for the road — great for camping, RVing, or heading to the beach. Lunch-box-size portable power stations like the Bluetti offer plenty of power, plus a combination of AC outlets and at least one USB-C Power Delivery (PD) port, letting you run laptops and other devices that don’t use a traditional wall plug alongside household appliances.
 With 288 watt hours of capacity, the Elite 30 V2 can run a full-size refrigerator for roughly three hours. At just 30 decibels — about as quiet as a library — it’s ideal for powering medical devices in a bedroom, where excess fan noise can be disruptive. Plugged into a wall outlet, the Bluetti recharges in about 70 minutes, can be charged using Bluetti’s 100W and 200W solar panels, and like many modern portable power stations, it can be monitored over Wi-Fi or Bluetooth so you can keep tabs on remaining power from your phone.
